Let us leave the camp now, and go back across the ditch, and around the walls, to the water on the northern side. This is the Golden Horn. A long, curved inlet of the sea that runs beside the city like a river somebody forgot to finish. It is deep, and it is sheltered, and it is the reason this city was built here and not somewhere else. On a calm night, the Horn is almost black. The water holds no light of its own. It only holds what is given to it ,  the lamps along the walls, the low moon, the small orange glow of a single boat. And across the mouth of this inlet, there is a chain. You would not think, from the sound of the word, that a chain could matter so much. But this one does. It is not a small thing ,  it is made of great iron links, and it is supported on wooden floats, so that it lies across the water like a line drawn by someone very patient. One end is fixed to a tower on the city walls. The other end is fixed to a tower on the far shore. When the chain is up, nothing comes in. When the chain is up, the city has a harbour that cannot be reached. And a harbour that cannot be reached is not a small advantage in a siege. Let us be clear about why. A city can be defended from the land. That is what walls are for. Walls are a promise: we will make you pay for every step. But a city cannot be fed from the land.

Not a city of this size, not with an army sitting on the fields outside. Bread does not grow on walls. Fish does not swim in a ditch. Everything that keeps a city alive comes by water. Grain from the Black Sea. Wine. Oil. Dried fish. Rope. Nails. Charcoal. Letters. People. So the defenders' whole hope rests on two things: that the wall holds, and that the water stays open. That is why the chain is there. That is why it is guarded. That is why, every evening, men walk along the floats with a lantern, checking the links, checking the ropes, checking that nothing has slipped. It is the least dramatic job in the city, and it is the one that matters most. Now. Let us look at the water inside the chain. There are ships here. Not many. Maybe twenty-six, of different sizes, some of them merchant vessels that came in before the siege and never left. Their sails are furled. Their decks are quiet. There are men asleep under the thwarts, and men on watch, and a lamp at the masthead of one ship that swings very slightly with the water. This is the last fleet of Constantinople. It is not a war fleet. It is a collection of whatever could float and be useful. And in the darkness beyond the chain, out on the open water of the Bosphorus, there are other ships. Many more. They are not moving. They are waiting. They have been waiting for weeks.

Here is the thing that nobody in the city can explain, and that the men on the wall talk about in low voices. The enemy has a fleet. The enemy has more men than the city has people. The enemy has money, and wood, and rope, and time. But the enemy cannot get past a chain. They have tried. They have rowed up to it in the dark, and been driven back by the ships inside and the archers on the walls. They have tried to burn it. They have tried to cut it. Each time, the chain has held. So for weeks, this has been the shape of the siege: an army that cannot get in by land, and a fleet that cannot get in by water. A stalemate made of stone and iron. Now let me tell you about the night the shape changed. And I want to tell it slowly, because the strangest things in history are usually the quietest. It happened in the last week of April. Not with a battle. Not with a bombardment. With a decision. The decision was this: if the ships cannot go over the chain, then the ships will go around it. Around it. Over the hill behind the far shore. Over land. I know how that sounds. It sounds like something a child would suggest, and an adult would laugh at. Ships are heavy. Hills are steep. And the far shore is not ours ,  it belongs to a Genoese colony called Galata, which is officially neutral and unofficially helpful to whoever is winning. But the decision was made.

And then, one night, the work began. Let us go and watch it. It is very late. There is no moon worth speaking of. On the slope behind Galata, between the cypress trees and the low walls of the vineyards, there is a line of men. Hundreds of them. They are not marching. They are crouched, and pulling, and sweating, and saying nothing. Between them and the water, there is a road. But it is not a road. It is a path made of planks, laid end to end, greased with fat and oil, so that a heavy thing can slide where it could never roll. From the shore, up the hill, over the crest, and down the other side into the Horn. And on those planks, moving very slowly, there are ships. Imagine the size of them. Not the great ships ,  the smaller ones, the ones that can be dragged. But even a small ship is thirty paces long, and wide as a house, and made of oak, and heavy with its own keel. Imagine the ropes. Imagine the men leaning into them, shoulder to shoulder, feet slipping on the greased wood. Imagine the sound: not shouting ,  they cannot shout, they must not be heard ,  but breathing. A hundred men breathing together. And under the breathing, the long, low groan of oak moving over fat. Imagine the oxen, and the men who walk beside the hull with wedges, pushing them under, taking them out, pushing them under again. And imagine the night, all around it. The dark.

The smell of pine tar and sweat and crushed grass. The lights of the city across the water, so close that a man could throw a stone at them, and so far that nothing can be done. They did this for two nights. Nobody in the city noticed. That is the part I want you to sit with. For two nights, seventy ships were dragged over a hill, within sight of the walls of Constantinople, and the people inside ,  the guards on the wall, the fishermen on the water, the men checking the chain ,  noticed nothing. Because it was quiet. Because it was slow. Because the most enormous thing in the world was happening a few hundred paces away, and it sounded like breathing. On the morning of the third day, a man on the wall looked out at the Golden Horn, the way he had looked out at it every morning of his life, and saw masts. Masts inside the chain. There is a kind of silence that comes after seeing something impossible. Not fear. Not yet. Just the mind refusing, for a moment, to connect one thing to another. He looked at the masts. He looked at the chain, still up, still unbroken. He looked back at the masts. And then he went to wake the others. Inside the city, that morning, something changed that no wall had managed to change in a thousand years. The water was no longer safe. That was all. That was the whole of it. Not a breach. Not a battle.

Just this: the one thing that had been certain, the one thing that had been true every single day of every single life in that city, was no longer true. You could no longer say: whatever happens, the sea is ours. Let us leave the Horn now. Let us walk back along the water, past the chain, past the quiet ships, up the stone steps, and into the city. There is a lamp burning in a window on the hill. Someone is awake. Someone always is. Let us go and see what they are doing. The answer to a wall is not a soldier. It is a machine. For a thousand years, the walls of Constantinople had been the best answer anyone had ever built to the question of how to keep an army out. And for a thousand years, the answer to the walls had been the same: you cannot. You can starve them. You can wait. You can try the gate at night. But you cannot knock the wall down. The stone is too thick. The men on the walls are too many. The ditch is too deep. That was true for eleven hundred years. Then someone invented a way to throw a very large stone a very long way, and everything that had been true stopped being true. Let us look at the machine. It is not beautiful. That is the first thing. We imagine great engines of war as elegant things ,  carved, symmetrical, clever. This is not elegant. It is a tube.

A tube of bronze, cast in one piece, so long that a man cannot reach from one end of it to the other with both arms wide. It rests in a cradle of heavy timber, and the timber rests on a bed of stone and packed earth, and the whole thing is held down with chains and stakes and iron bands. It is so large that it had to be built where it stands. It could not be carried. It could only be dragged, and even dragging it took sixty oxen and a road built for the purpose. The man who made it is not a soldier. He is a founder. His name is Urban ,  or something close to it, because names travel badly across languages ,  and he came to the city a year earlier, and offered his invention to the emperor. The emperor had no money. Not the kind of money this would take. So Urban went to the other side of the water, and offered it to the sultan. The sultan had money. I want you to notice something about this. It is not a moral. It is just a fact, and it is the sort of fact that this whole night is made of. A city runs out of money. A man crosses the water. A machine changes sides. Nobody in this story is a villain. Everybody is doing a job, in the way that people do jobs, for whoever can pay for the work. The gun is fired by a team. There are perhaps a hundred men around it, though only a few of them touch it.

There are men who carry the powder in wooden tubs lined with leather, and men who pack it with a wooden rammer, slowly and carefully, because a spark in the wrong place would kill everyone in the ring. There are men who bring the stone. The stone is the part I want to describe, because it is easy to forget. It is not a small ball. It is a sphere cut from marble ,  or from granite, on the days when the marble runs out ,  so large that a man cannot put his arms around it, and so heavy that it takes a cart to bring it to the gun, and a crane to lift it into the mouth. And here is the thing that is so strange that it is almost tender: the stones were made somewhere else, and brought here. The best ones came by sea, from an island in the Marmara. They were cut, and smoothed, and loaded onto boats, and sailed across the water in the night, to be fired at the city they came from. Now let us stand here for a moment, and think about the firing. There is a flash. That is the obvious part, and it is over quickly. The sound comes later. That is the part nobody expects. The sound of a great gun is not a bang. It is a blow. It hits you in the chest, and it goes on hitting you for a long time after the flash is gone, rolling out across the water and coming back off the hills, so that for a few seconds it is hard to tell which direction it came from.

And then there is the dust. After the sound, the air in front of the gun is full of dust, and the dust does not settle. It hangs, and it drifts, and it makes the whole morning the colour of a road. The men around the gun do not cheer. They are already working. Someone is swabbing the bore with a wet cloth on a long pole ,  slowly, carefully, because this is the most dangerous moment of the whole process. Someone is measuring powder. Someone is walking out to look at where the stone went. They will do this again in an hour. And again after that. Let us walk to the wall now, and look from the other side. This is harder. The men on the wall have been hearing this sound for weeks. They have learned to tell the great gun from the smaller ones. They have learned which sections of wall it is aiming at, and which of them are likely to be standing under it. They have also learned what the stone does. It does not knock a hole, the way we imagine. It does something slower. The stone strikes the face of the wall, and the face of the wall crumbles. Not much ,  a few arms' lengths of stone, a section of facing, a great deal of dust. Then the next stone comes, an hour later, and crumbles a little more. And the next. And under the facing, there is rubble. And under the rubble, there is earth. And the earth moves.

That is what the men on the wall notice, and what they cannot stop. The wall is not being broken. It is being loosened. Every night, they go out with baskets and barrels, and they fill the gaps, and they prop the loose stone with timber, and they build back a little of what the day took away. Every night, they do this in the dark, while the guns are quiet, with the sound of their own shovels very loud in the silence. Every morning, the guns begin again. There is one more thing to say about the guns, and then we will leave them. They are not perfect. This is easy to forget, because we tell this story knowing how it ends. But on this night ,  the night of the twenty-eighth of May ,  the great gun is broken. The mouth has split. That happens to bronze when it is asked to do more than bronze wants to do. The crack runs back from the lip, and every shot widens it, and the men who work it know that one day it will simply come apart in their hands. So they have been repairing it. In the dark, on the ground, in the dirt, with iron rings heated red and hammered on, and ropes, and a great deal of argument. They will finish tonight. I do not want you to think of this as a triumph. It is not a triumph. It is a group of tired men, in a field, in the dark, trying to make a broken thing work one more time. We do that too. All of us.

At some point in our lives, we are the men in the field with the broken thing, deciding whether it is worth another hour. Let us go back into the city now. The lamps are still lit. There is still a little time.
